articles.title: Petalburg takes the division; Rustboro takes the harder road
articles.dek: Flygon intercepted Shawn Watzon twice, Iron Valiant threw two touchdowns, and a 17–10 road win secured Hoenn West. Oinkologne’s three-week absence complicates the celebration.
articles.author: tessa-wren

body.text: Petalburg won Hoenn West with a third-down touchdown and a defense that made Rustboro’s final passing chances expensive. Iron Valiant found Parasect for four yards with 2:38 left in the third quarter, Flygon intercepted Shawn Watzon for the second time late in the fourth, and the Pride left Rustboro with a 17–10 victory and a division championship. At 11–5, Petalburg has moved beyond the reach of both the Stone and Dewford with one regular-season game remaining.

Rustboro is 9–7 and still has a playoff berth. That distinction matters after a defeat with several preventable costs. The Stone can improve their wild-card position against Dewford in the finale, but they will begin the postseason on the road. Petalburg will host a first-round game. The teams finished with eleven first downs apiece and only eleven yards separating their total offense; the consequences of their mistakes were much farther apart.

Iron Valiant completed fifteen of twenty-four passes for 157 yards, two touchdowns and no interceptions. Watzon finished eighteen of thirty-two for 205 yards, one touchdown and two interceptions. Flygon made both of those takeaways, returning the first twenty-seven yards and ending the second at the interception spot. Petalburg committed no turnovers. In a game with twenty-seven combined points, those extra possessions gave the visitors the decisive advantage.

“The throw to Parasect was there because everybody did the ordinary work before it,” Iron Valiant said. “I didn’t need to make the play bigger. I needed to complete it.” The quarterback’s account fits a performance that produced relatively little spectacle and exactly enough scoring. His two touchdown passes went to different receivers; neither required Petalburg to sustain the kind of passing volume that Rustboro managed through Gibby Timmy.
Two interceptions with different jobs

The first quarter ended scoreless. Petalburg opened the scoring at 5:57 of the second when Iron Valiant threw deep over the middle to Golbat for a twelve-yard touchdown. Sunflora supplied the extra point. Rustboro answered with Gorebyss’s fifty-three-yard field goal, then moved ahead on Watzon’s three-yard pass to Watchog with thirty-five seconds left before halftime. The Stone had turned a quiet opening into a 10–7 lead.

body.alt: Iron Valiant #21, Golbat #10. Iron Valiant found Golbat for a twelve-yard touchdown in the second quarter. Illustrated from the recorded play.
body.caption: Iron Valiant found Golbat for a twelve-yard touchdown in the second quarter. Illustrated from the recorded play.

body.text: Petalburg still had time to respond. Sunflora’s forty-yard field goal with six seconds remaining tied the game at ten, taking away Rustboro’s opportunity to enter the break ahead. Both kickers had demonstrated useful range. The second-half difference would come through the passing game, although it was a defender who created the most valuable change in possession.

At 3:29 of the third quarter, Watzon’s short-left throw was intercepted by Flygon and returned twenty-seven yards. Watzon made the tackle. Less than a minute of game time later, Iron Valiant faced third-and-three and completed the short-left touchdown to Parasect. Sunflora’s conversion made it 17–10. The Pride had converted the first interception into the only points either team would score after halftime.

Flygon’s second interception came with 1:37 remaining, on a deep-right throw from Watzon. Gibby Timmy stopped the return immediately. The two plays demonstrate why a return-yard total alone can understate a defender’s influence: the first takeaway improved Petalburg’s scoring opportunity, while the second removed a late Rustboro opportunity. Both served the same seven-point lead in different ways.

Petalburg also recorded eight pass breakups to Rustboro’s four. The Stone were not overwhelmed by sacks; each quarterback took one. Coverage and ball placement became the more consequential contest. Watzon had thrown only two season interceptions entering this game, making the pair here especially costly. A usually careful passer supplied the kind of opening Petalburg’s defense needed against a receiving threat that otherwise kept producing.
Gibby’s yards could not supply a second touchdown

Gibby Timmy caught seven passes on thirteen targets for 145 yards. His longest reception gained thirty-one. The receiver accounted for most of Rustboro’s passing production, giving Watzon a consistent destination even as the Pride interrupted other attempts. SEARED BITE added twenty-four yards on three catches; Roggenrola had seventeen on two. Watchog’s lone reception became the Stone’s touchdown.

The imbalance left Rustboro dependent on a relatively narrow route to scoring. Philly Gabite carried thirteen times for forty-four yards, while Watchog added ten yards on three runs. Watzon contributed fourteen rushing yards, bringing the team total to sixty-eight. The Stone converted three of ten third downs. Their passing yardage kept the game close, but the running game supplied too few uncomplicated advances to make every possession easier.

Tyler Scarboro described the afternoon in the manner of a professor who has found the same arithmetic error in several papers. “You can carry the ball all the way across the county and still come home without the groceries,” he said. “We had yards. We had chances. We gave two chances to Flygon, and he didn’t give them back.” The diagnosis was blunt enough without pretending that the Stone had failed to move the ball at all.

body.alt: Porygon-Z #37. Shawn Watzon threw for 205 yards, one touchdown and two interceptions. An imagined sideline portrait.
body.caption: Shawn Watzon threw for 205 yards, one touchdown and two interceptions. An imagined sideline portrait.

body.text: Rustboro outgained Petalburg 273–262. That is a useful corrective to any account that makes this a comprehensive rout. The Stone had a productive primary receiver, a long field goal and a defense that forced six punts. They also missed one of two field-goal attempts and finished with one touchdown. Petalburg’s defense repeatedly made Rustboro work again after the gains that appeared to be opening the game.
The division comes with a backfield problem

Oinkologne gave the Pride eighty-nine rushing yards on just five carries, including a thirty-seven-yard run, and added a thirty-yard reception. Those six touches generated 119 yards. His production was particularly important because Whiscash finished with minus-two rushing yards on twelve attempts. Petalburg’s team rushing total of 105 therefore describes a sharp difference between its available runners, rather than consistent success on every series.

Oinkologne now carries a three-week injury designation. The report does not identify the moment of injury, and the game’s touch totals do not establish when his work stopped. What is clear is the size of the contribution Petalburg must replace for the finale and potentially beyond it. A division title gives the Pride a home playoff game; it does not guarantee the return of their most productive runner from this win.

Farigiraf led Petalburg’s receivers with forty-five yards on two catches. Golbat supplied thirty yards and the opening touchdown, while Parasect’s only catch became the winning score. Vikavolt caught five passes for twenty-five yards. Iron Valiant spread his completions across a broad group, but Oinkologne’s thirty-yard reception remained one of the largest pieces of the passing total as well as his rushing contribution.

Norman can acknowledge the achievement while preparing for that absence. “The division belongs to this group because they kept finishing difficult games,” he said. “Now somebody has to take the next set of carries seriously. We’ll enjoy what we earned and then get specific.” Seviper’s remaining injury counter has reached zero, offering a relevant receiving development without establishing a future snap assignment or making Oinkologne’s absence disappear.

Petalburg closes against Mauville, whose playoff position remains unsettled. Rustboro hosts Dewford in a game that determines the ordering of two confirmed wild cards. Those are substantial assignments for both clubs. The Pride can still affect their seed among the division winners, and the Stone can still improve their first-round matchup, even though the division question has been answered.

The finale against Mauville will also influence the wild-card field. Petalburg already has its championship, but the visiting Dynamos can secure the last conference berth with a win. Norman therefore prepares for an opponent with an immediate postseason objective while working through the loss of Oinkologne. The division-clinching result settles one question and leaves several practical lineup decisions for the following week.

For Petalburg, the immediate accomplishment is concrete: eleven wins, Hoenn West secured, and a postseason game at home. Rustboro’s immediate work is equally concrete: turn productive receiving into more than one touchdown, keep the ball away from the opposing secondary, and recover against a Dewford team that has already secured its own berth. Flygon’s two interceptions ensured that the division trophy would not wait for that final round.

art.alt: Iron Valiant #21. Iron Valiant led Petalburg to the Hoenn West title. An editorial tunnel portrait.

articles.title: Five touchdowns from Moth Ball put Johto East on the final game
articles.dek: Lavender beat Violet 51–10 behind Moth Ball, Hobbes and four interceptions. Beat Blackthorn next, and the Wails take the division.
articles.author: ellis-quill

body.text: Lavender’s replacement quarterback has acquired a nickname and a much larger assignment. Moth Ball, the Frosmoth who has been carrying the passing game during Mr. Clanky’s absence, threw five touchdown passes in a 51–10 win at Violet. The Wails improved to 11–5 and will host Blackthorn with Johto East at stake. A Lavender victory takes the division; a Blackthorn win or tie keeps it with the Dragons.

That prospect gives the afternoon a significance beyond fifty-one points. Lavender has a playoff berth secured and can now earn a home game by beating the team immediately above it. Violet fell to 8–8 and needs help to reach the postseason. The same game that gave the Wails control of their division opportunity made the Falcons’ final week much more dependent on other results.

Moth Ball completed twenty-one of thirty-seven passes for 300 yards without an interception or a sack. Hobbes ran eighteen times for 116 yards and two touchdowns. Lavender’s defense intercepted Iron Jugulis four times and added a safety, creating enough separation that the visitors scored twenty-eight unanswered points after halftime. Violet finished with 201 total yards against Lavender’s 425.

“We can talk about the next game now, right?” Moth Ball said. “Good. I’ve already got questions.” His eagerness fits the pace of his recent promotion, but the performance contained more than enthusiasm. Five touchdown passes went to four receivers, and he avoided the turnover that might have given Violet a sustained recovery. Travis Scarboro’s response was shorter: “Good decisions. Some missed throws. Blackthorn next.”
Violet briefly made the score uncomfortable

Lavender’s opening advantage began with the defense. Dugtrio intercepted a short-right pass with 4:58 left in the first quarter and returned it thirty-eight yards out of bounds. Hobbes scored from one yard out at 3:50. Moth Ball then found Might Guy deep left for a twenty-four-yard touchdown at 1:48, and Maractus’s extra point made it 14–0.

Violet answered at the start of the second quarter. Iron Jugulis completed a fourteen-yard touchdown over the middle to Furret, and Loudred added a forty-four-yard field goal at 4:00. The Falcons had reduced the deficit to four points. For a team that would eventually lose by forty-one, that passage deserves its place in the account: Violet had a realistic game before Lavender’s pressure and takeaways expanded it.

The Wails changed the terms again with 1:54 left before halftime. Muk sacked Iron Jugulis for a seven-yard loss and a safety, pushing Lavender ahead 16–10. Octillery then intercepted a short-left pass at 0:57 and returned it thirteen yards. Moth Ball found The Wail deep right for a fourteen-yard touchdown at 0:36. Lavender reached halftime ahead 23–10.

Those two defensive events produced a particularly difficult sequence for Violet. The safety added points directly; the interception gave Lavender another possession before the break. The Wails did not need to invent a different offensive identity to exploit it. Moth Ball completed the scoring throw to a receiver who would finish with only thirty yards, showing how much a well-timed catch can matter within a modest total.
Four receivers finished the passing work

Might Guy led Lavender with 122 receiving yards on four catches. His forty-six-yard long reception and twenty-four-yard touchdown gave the passing game a deeper dimension, although five of his nine targets were not completed. Moth Ball could pursue those larger gains because other receivers kept supplying shorter completions. The offense did not require every deep attempt to work.

body.alt: Lucario #50. Might Guy gained 122 yards on four catches, including a twenty-four-yard touchdown. Illustrated from the recorded touchdown.
body.caption: Might Guy gained 122 yards on four catches, including a twenty-four-yard touchdown. Illustrated from the recorded touchdown.

body.text: Luvdisc caught eleven of fourteen targets for 101 yards and two touchdowns. The first score came on a one-yard short-right pass late in the third quarter. The second was an eighteen-yard deep-right completion in the fourth. The receiver’s total combined repeated availability with scoring work at two different distances, an important distinction from a hundred-yard day built around one isolated long gain.

“There were enough throws to go around,” Luvdisc said. “When one came my way, I wanted to give it somewhere safe to finish.” The modest explanation leaves out how often that happened. Eleven receptions accounted for more than half of Lavender’s completions. Against a defense trying to recover from turnovers, that reliable target helped Moth Ball maintain the offense without asking each possession to produce another spectacular play.

body.alt: Luvdisc #14. Luvdisc caught eleven passes for 101 yards and two touchdowns. An editorial receiving illustration.
body.caption: Luvdisc caught eleven passes for 101 yards and two touchdowns. An editorial receiving illustration.

body.text: The Wail added a touchdown among three receptions, and Unfezant scored on a seven-yard short-left pass early in the fourth quarter. Hobbes caught a thirty-yard pass in addition to his rushing work. Those contributions gave Lavender several ways to finish, including the two rushing touchdowns that prevented the scoreboard from becoming solely a record of Moth Ball’s passing afternoon.
The second half closed quickly

Hobbes scored on a seven-yard run up the middle with 2:46 remaining in the third. Four seconds of game time after the ensuing extra point, Iron Jugulis was intercepted by Mimikyu on a short-left pass. The return gained twenty yards. Lavender’s next touchdown came through Luvdisc at 1:17, stretching a comfortable advantage into a very difficult recovery assignment for the Falcons.

Noctowl intercepted another pass at 0:35 of the third, this time over the short middle. Lavender followed with Unfezant’s fourth-quarter touchdown, then Moth Ball’s second scoring connection with Luvdisc. The four interceptions belonged to four different defenders: Dugtrio, Octillery, Mimikyu and Noctowl. The distribution matters because Violet could not reduce the problem to avoiding one particular defender.

Iron Jugulis finished fifteen of twenty-nine for 128 yards, one touchdown and four interceptions. Violet converted three of nine third downs and punted four times. Zangoose supplied fifty-one rushing yards on five carries, but now has a four-week injury designation. His production had been one of the few efficient parts of the Falcons’ offense; the final-round preparation must account for his absence without inventing a replacement’s workload.

Lavender’s passing protection deserves credit alongside the scoring receivers. Moth Ball took no sacks while attempting thirty-seven passes. The Wails were five of ten on third down and committed no turnovers. Those facts help explain how the offense could keep adding points despite sixteen incomplete passes and three punts. It had enough unsuccessful snaps to correct, but very few that handed Violet an immediate scoring opportunity.

Scarboro remained characteristically economical when asked whether the result changed his view of the division race. “It gave us eleven wins,” he said. “The next one decides the division.” That is an accurate description of the standings and a useful limit on celebration. Lavender has earned the chance to settle the matter at home. It has not already won the game that settles it.

Blackthorn will arrive after beating Mahogany 27–19, with Hatterene producing 275 passing yards and two touchdown passes. The Dragons have a new two-week absence for Exploud. Lavender still has Mr. Clanky’s continuing absence to manage. The matchup will test whether the Wails’ current passing combination can repeat its useful work against a division rival with a much stronger record than Violet.

Violet’s last opponent is Mahogany, while Olivine travels to Azalea. The Falcons need Olivine to fail to win, but the exact requirement depends on both results: a Violet win passes an Olivine tie or loss, and a Violet tie is enough only with an Olivine loss. A defeat eliminates the Falcons. That distinction matters for a club whose record still leaves more than one possible route. The offense must prepare to improve on its 128 passing yards while accounting for Zangoose’s absence. Lavender, meanwhile, can complete its division pursuit without help elsewhere: beating Blackthorn at home is sufficient. Those contrasting final assignments give both staffs a specific reason to study the same game carefully.

The Falcons host Mahogany and must avoid defeat while watching the other Kanto–Johto wild-card results. A tie works only with an Olivine loss. Their immediate task is to reduce the passing mistakes that turned a 14–10 game into a 51–10 finish. Lavender’s task is more direct. After an afternoon in which a replacement quarterback threw five touchdowns and four defenders intercepted passes, the Wails can win their division by winning one more game.

art.alt: Frosmoth #15. Moth Ball threw five touchdown passes as Lavender moved within one victory of a division title.

articles.title: Budew wins his start, Crox brings the pressure, and Mossdeep reaches 16–0
articles.dek: The Eclipse beat Sootopolis 22–3 behind seven sacks and two Budew Baker touchdown passes. Poury Holt’s seven-week injury designation changes the backfield outlook.
articles.author: mara-voss

body.text: Budew Baker threw a touchdown to Jelly Hurts, Fletcher Crox collected three sacks, and Mossdeep won its sixteenth consecutive game with a lineup that gave several younger players meaningful work. The 22–3 victory over Sootopolis preserved the Eclipse’s unbeaten record and left one regular-season trip, to Lavaridge, between them and a perfect finish. Their conference’s first seed and bye were already secure.

The most difficult consequence came through the injury report. Poury Holt rushed for 115 yards on sixteen carries and added a five-yard reception, then emerged with a seven-week designation. The report does not identify when the injury happened. His production was a major part of the win, and his absence now changes the available backfield for the final regular-season game and the postseason run ahead.

Mossdeep still held Sootopolis to 136 total yards and six first downs. The Eclipse recorded seven sacks, forced seven punts and allowed no touchdowns. Baker completed sixteen of thirty passes for 166 yards, two touchdowns and one interception. The offense produced twenty first downs and 170 rushing yards, giving the young quarterback enough support to win despite three sacks and several unfinished passing opportunities.

Michael Dorrill was asked whether sixteen wins permitted a more relaxed review. “We lost a fumble, threw an interception and punted twice,” he said. “Which one did you want me to congratulate?” He could recognize Baker’s successful start and still insist on the corrections. The score gave Mossdeep a comfortable result; it did not remove the evidence that the offense had left work unfinished.
Baker’s first score went to another developing passer

The opening touchdown arrived with forty-eight seconds left in the first quarter. Baker, playing in his Roselia form, threw short left to Jelly Hurts for seven yards. The Solosis’s only catch became a touchdown, and Adam Vinathorn supplied the extra point. Two players more often discussed through future possibilities had combined for the first seven points of an actual league win.

body.alt: Solosis #10. Jelly Hurts caught Baker’s seven-yard touchdown pass with forty-eight seconds left in the first quarter. Illustrated from the recorded play.
body.caption: Jelly Hurts caught Baker’s seven-yard touchdown pass with forty-eight seconds left in the first quarter. Illustrated from the recorded play.

body.text: Baker’s second touchdown came much later, with 3:24 left in the fourth quarter. He found Ninjulio Jones short left for thirteen yards, moving Mossdeep beyond any realistic late Sootopolis recovery. The scores bracketed a game in which the Eclipse repeatedly benefited from their defense while the offense worked through an uneven passing afternoon. Both completions mattered, and neither erases the attempts that failed between them.

Ninjulio caught three passes on ten targets for thirty yards. Driflon Diggs was more efficient, catching four of five targets for sixty-four yards, including a twenty-four-yard gain. Will Shells added thirty-three yards on three catches. Reggie Bite caught three for twenty-one. Those receiving lines describe a quarterback who found help across the formation while still leaving several intended connections incomplete.

“I wanted the second touchdown because we still had a job to finish,” Baker said. “Winning the start doesn’t make the interception acceptable.” The determination fits his performance better than an exaggerated declaration that the quarterback hierarchy has permanently changed. Dram Marino’s established season production remains part of Mossdeep’s larger picture. This game established that Baker could complete a winning start with the available support around him.
Seven sacks kept Sootopolis from building drives

Crox finished with three sacks and eight pressures. The Sandile’s work was the largest individual part of a pass rush that repeatedly removed yards from Sootopolis possessions. Clay Rathews, Derrat Brooks, Reggie Bite and Champ Baeley each supplied another sack. Drampa was sacked seven times for thirty-nine yards of losses, a severe burden for an offense that completed only eleven passes.

body.alt: Sandile #99. Fletcher Crox recorded three sacks and eight pressures. An editorial pass-rush illustration.
body.caption: Fletcher Crox recorded three sacks and eight pressures. An editorial pass-rush illustration.

body.text: Brooks delivered the most directly valuable sack. With 4:25 remaining in the third quarter, he brought Drampa down for a six-yard loss and a safety. Mossdeep had led 10–3 at halftime. The safety made it 12–3, and Vinathorn added a forty-one-yard field goal later in the quarter. The Eclipse increased their advantage without requiring Baker to force a touchdown throw into a difficult situation.

Sootopolis converted two of ten third downs. Rillaboom gained thirty-five yards on nine carries, while the team finished with forty-one rushing yards. Drampa threw for ninety-five yards without an interception, but avoiding a giveaway did not solve the protection problem. The Surge could retain possession through an individual play and still lose the series when sacks and incomplete passes made the next down harder.

Pawmo caught four passes for sixty-three yards, including a twenty-yard gain. The rest of the receiving group combined for thirty-two yards. Two receptions lost a yard apiece. Mossdeep’s defense therefore limited both the number of productive targets and the frequency with which Sootopolis could repeat its successful plays. Seven punts are a useful summary of that work, but the six first downs explain it more clearly.
The turnovers gave Dorrill specific material

Holt fumbled on a one-yard run left early in the second quarter. Runerigus recovered for Sootopolis. The Surge’s points came on Vikavolt’s thirty-five-yard field goal at 4:39, reducing the deficit to 7–3. Mossdeep’s defense prevented a touchdown, but the offense had still created an unnecessary opportunity. Dorrill does not need a loss to identify a possession that should have lasted longer.

Baker’s interception came with 1:29 left in the third quarter. A deep-middle attempt was intercepted by Drifblim and returned ten yards before Holt made the tackle. Mossdeep already led 15–3, so the throw did not reverse the game. It did give the coaching staff a concrete late-game decision to review with a quarterback learning how to manage an advantage as well as create one.

The Eclipse also had useful responses that deserve equal specificity. Vinathorn made both field-goal attempts, from forty-seven and forty-one yards, and both extra points. Mossdeep converted five of ten third downs. The offense accumulated 336 total yards against 136 allowed. Those advantages made the mistakes survivable and gave Baker repeated chances to return to a functional possession rather than chase a growing deficit.

Shawn Mareman ran eight times for forty-eight yards and caught a six-yard pass. Ninjulio added a six-yard carry, and Baker gained one net yard on two attempts. Holt’s 115 yards remained the largest piece of the rushing total, but the other contributions show why his absence should be discussed through actual available work rather than a vague assurance that somebody will replace everything.
A perfect record and a changed injury report

Holt’s seven-week designation is the central availability development. Richard Furman’s remaining injury counter has reached zero, although he remains on injured reserve in the current roster record. That counter does not establish activation or a future role. Marshall Flock’s game report listed a minor issue. None of those entries justifies inventing a medical diagnosis or promising who will carry the ball in the next game.

Gyarls Woodson also reached Gyarados after the game, an important development for a player who had been progressing as Magikarp. The evolution belongs to the postgame record. It should not be inserted into the Sootopolis play log as though a Gyarados had produced the afternoon’s earlier snaps. Mossdeep’s younger players have enough actual developments to discuss without moving them backward in time.

The Eclipse have now scored 697 points and allowed 130 through sixteen games. Their record places them above every remaining Hoenn–Sinnoh seeding dispute. Lavaridge’s final-round incentive is different, and the Inferno’s recent wins require their own preparation. Mossdeep can pursue a seventeenth victory while deciding how to distribute work among the players available after Holt’s injury.

The final trip to Lavaridge is Mossdeep’s chance to finish the regular season unbeaten. Its first seed and bye are already secure, so preparation can account for both the next game and the confirmed absences beyond it.

Dorrill’s review will have a clear sequence: the fumble, the interception, the sacks allowed, the incomplete connections, then the work that produced the win. Baker has a successful start to examine. Crox has three sacks. The defense has another game without an opposing touchdown. Mossdeep’s next assignment is to carry those useful performances into the finale with a backfield that has lost a substantial contributor.

art.alt: Roselia #37. Budew Baker threw two touchdown passes in Mossdeep’s 22–3 victory.

articles.title: Crem throws for 318 as Mt. Silver locks down the bye
articles.dek: The Reds answered their Cinnabar defeat with a 41–9 win at Azalea and secured the conference’s first seed. Tony Gyarzalez’s six-week absence changes the receiving picture.
articles.author: dorian-pike

body.text: Mt. Silver has the first seed, the first-round bye and a quarterback performance worth discussing at full volume. Crem Ftzpatrik completed twenty-seven of thirty-seven passes for 318 yards and three touchdowns as the Reds beat Azalea 41–9. The win improved them to 14–2 and secured the top of Kanto–Johto before the final regular-season round. Connor McLarren will get a postseason week off whether or not anybody likes his jokes.

There is substantial work attached to that privilege. Tony Gyarzalez caught five passes for fifty-six yards and now has a six-week injury designation. Ninjask has a new two-week absence. The Reds can prepare from the best position in the conference while acknowledging that two unavailable players have changed the group around their passing game. A bye gives them time; it does not manufacture healthy receiving production.

Ftzpatrik’s afternoon supplied an encouraging starting point. The Alcremie threw touchdown passes to Scep Smith Jr., Roselia and Plusico Buress, took no sacks and helped an offense that never punted. Garshawn Lynch added 107 rushing yards and two touchdowns. Mt. Silver produced 453 total yards against 151 and twenty-two first downs against five. Those are substantial answers after allowing thirty-eight points at Cinnabar.

McLarren allowed himself a small smile. “They told me the offense needed a response,” he said. “I thought three touchdown passes and no punts was a fairly legible one.” He also had an interception and a lost fumble to review. The Reds won by thirty-two because their defense made those mistakes manageable, not because the mistakes ceased to exist when the scoreboard became pleasant.
A clean pocket gave Crem a full afternoon

Ftzpatrik had entered the previous game in relief and now supplied the complete passing line. His thirty-seven attempts produced twenty-seven completions, a completion rate just under seventy-three percent. The absence of sacks matters as much as the raw yardage: Mt. Silver could keep operating its offense without repeatedly surrendering yards before the ball reached a receiver. The passing game was productive from its first scoring connection through its third.

Scep Smith Jr. caught six passes for 108 yards, including a forty-five-yard touchdown on a short-left throw at 5:07 of the second quarter. The play supplied the largest gain in his receiving line and stretched the lead to two touchdowns after the extra point. Calling the throw short preserves an important part of the account. The completed play gained forty-five yards; that does not mean the ball traveled forty-five yards before the catch.

body.alt: Sceptile #11. Scep Smith Jr. turned a short-left completion into a forty-five-yard touchdown. Illustrated from the recorded play.
body.caption: Scep Smith Jr. turned a short-left completion into a forty-five-yard touchdown. Illustrated from the recorded play.

body.text: Plusico Buress caught eight passes on ten targets for fifty yards and a touchdown. The catches were shorter, but the repeat availability was useful. Gyarzalez added fifty-six yards on five catches, Gregar Jenings had forty-one on two, and Lynch contributed another forty-one receiving yards. Ftzpatrik could distribute the ball without forcing all of the offense through the longest-gain receiver.

“There were a lot of good places to put it,” Ftzpatrik said. “I’m glad I found enough of them.” That is a characteristically restrained account of a 318-yard start. Scep Smith Jr. had less interest in shrinking his part. “If the throw gets to me, I expect us to go somewhere,” he said. The two descriptions can coexist: careful distribution from the quarterback and an assertive receiver turning a short throw into a major score.
Lynch finished at the goal line

Lynch opened the scoring with a one-yard run left at 3:51 of the first quarter. His second touchdown came on another one-yard carry, up the middle at the start of the fourth. Between those scores he gained useful yardage without needing an enormous single run; his longest rush was thirteen yards. Seventeen carries produced 107 yards, a little more than six per attempt.

Vibrava added twenty-nine yards on five carries. Ftzpatrik lost a yard on his one rushing attempt, leaving Mt. Silver with 135 rushing yards as a team. The combination of a productive lead back, usable secondary carries and an efficient passing game allowed the Reds to sustain possessions through different parts of the formation. Azalea could not solve the afternoon by concentrating on one type of play.

Lynch also lost a fumble at 0:21 of the first quarter after a ten-yard run up the middle. Gliscor recovered for Azalea. The turnover is worth retaining alongside the two touchdowns because it identifies a real correction within a successful afternoon. A runner can be decisive in a win and still leave the coaching staff a specific possession to revisit.

“I liked the touchdowns better,” Lynch said, with the cheerful certainty of a player who had contributed two of them. “I’m guessing everybody else did too.” McLarren will likely agree with the preference and spend more meeting time on the fumble. Mt. Silver’s defense ensured that the error did not change control of the game, but playoff opponents may offer less room for another lost possession.

body.alt: Garchomp #22. Garshawn Lynch scored twice on short runs and finished with 107 rushing yards. An editorial goal-line illustration.
body.caption: Garshawn Lynch scored twice on short runs and finished with 107 rushing yards. An editorial goal-line illustration.

body.text: Azalea could not convert a third down

The Swarm finished zero for eleven on third down. Drampa completed eleven of thirty passes for 122 yards, and Azalea managed twenty-nine rushing yards on ten attempts. Six punts repeatedly returned the ball to an offense that was already moving it well. The Reds recorded one sack and eight pass breakups, limiting the passing game without needing a large sack total to make every possession difficult.

Azalea’s points came entirely from Sunflora’s field goals, from thirty-four, twenty-six and twenty-six yards. The first two arrived late in the second quarter. Ftzpatrik’s interception, a deep-right attempt picked by Gliscor at 0:54, gave the Swarm another opportunity before halftime. Azalea converted it into three points, leaving Mt. Silver ahead 21–6 rather than allowing the error to become a much larger interruption.

Gliscor recovered the fumble and made the interception, supplying Azalea with two valuable defensive moments. The offense could not turn that help into a touchdown. Drampa avoided interceptions, but nineteen incomplete passes and the third-down failures prevented the Swarm from sustaining enough work around their occasional gains. Vivillon’s thirty-nine-yard reception was their largest receiving play and only catch in six targets.

Mt. Silver went five of eight on third down. The comparison is direct: one offense repeatedly extended possessions; the other repeatedly reached a fourth-down decision. Weepinbell made field goals from forty and twenty-nine yards in the final quarter and converted all five extra points. The Reds could add points from their later opportunities while Azalea remained scoreless throughout that period.
The bye changes preparation, not availability

Gyarzalez’s six-week absence deserves more attention than the comfortable margin might otherwise permit. His five catches were a useful part of Ftzpatrik’s distribution, and his season work has made him an established receiving option. The current report offers a duration, not a guaranteed postseason return. The Reds must prepare for the players available to them rather than count on a calendar outcome that has not occurred.

Ninjask’s two-week designation is shorter but still relevant to the remaining schedule. Mt. Silver’s secured bye reduces its immediate game load after the finale, although that fact alone should not be translated into a confirmed return date. The next depth choices belong to McLarren’s preparation. This game demonstrates which receivers contributed at Azalea; it does not announce how every future target will be reassigned.

The Reds host Cianwood in Week 18. The Crushers remain alive for a wild card and have just beaten Olivine 10–3, so the visitor’s incentive will be considerable. Mt. Silver can choose its preparation with the first seed secured, but Cianwood’s situation gives the game a consequence beyond the favorite’s record. The Reds’ own standard is to carry a useful passing performance into that assignment.

Fourteen wins have now bought Mt. Silver home-field priority in its conference and a free first-round weekend. Ftzpatrik has supplied a complete, productive start. Lynch has passed a hundred rushing yards again. The defense has held an opponent without a third-down conversion. McLarren has earned the position from which to make his next decisions, and the new injury report tells him exactly why those decisions still require care.

art.alt: Alcremie #12. Crem Ftzpatrik threw for 318 yards and three touchdowns as Mt. Silver secured the first seed.

articles.title: Saffron keeps its balance and secures the second seed
articles.dek: Dam Skattebo scored twice, Archam Manning threw two touchdowns, and the Psi Corps beat Cerulean 31–13. A kickoff fumble helped break the game open.
articles.author: rowan-vale

body.text: Saffron followed seventy points with thirty-one, which I am prepared to accept as a reasonable week at the office. Dam Skattebo ran for two touchdowns, Archam Manning threw for two more, and the Psi Corps beat Cerulean 31–13 to improve to 13–3. The Kanto East champions secured the conference’s second seed with this victory. Mt. Silver owns the bye; Saffron owns a first-round game at home and a defense that has allowed 128 points all season.

Cerulean is 7–9 and still has a narrow route into the final wild-card place. The Tide’s next game against Vermilion therefore carries stakes that this loss could not extinguish by itself. It did make the route more demanding. Saffron controlled the useful offensive volume, producing twenty-two first downs to nine and running fifty-nine offensive plays against Cerulean’s thirty-one.

Manning completed twenty-two of thirty-three passes for 287 yards, two touchdowns and no interceptions. Skattebo carried nineteen times for sixty-eight yards and two short scores. Saffron finished with an even hundred rushing yards, 387 total yards and no turnovers. The Psi Corps did not reproduce last week’s extraordinary receiving eruption, but they gave Trent Scarboro plenty of productive work to celebrate.

“They came back and did the work again,” Scarboro said. “Different game, different chances, same responsibility to each other.” His enthusiasm has a measurable basis. Saffron converted four of seven third downs, allowed one sack and finished four touchdown opportunities with four successful extra points. A team that had just scored seventy could have become impatient with ordinary drives. This one kept using them.

body.alt: Alakazam #6. Archam Manning completed twenty-two passes for 287 yards and two touchdowns. An editorial passing illustration.
body.caption: Archam Manning completed twenty-two passes for 287 yards and two touchdowns. An editorial passing illustration.

body.text: Skattebo supplied the first two touchdowns

The opening score came at 3:30 of the first quarter, when Skattebo ran two yards up the middle. Octillery’s conversion made it 7–0. Cerulean answered at the start of the second quarter with a twenty-three-yard short-right touchdown pass from Farigiraf to Zebstrika, but the missed extra point left the Tide a point behind. The visitors then returned to the same reliable finishing method.

At 3:23 of the second, Skattebo scored on a three-yard run up the middle on third down. Octillery’s extra point struck the upright and still went through. Saffron led 14–6. The two rushing touchdowns are useful context for a game in which Manning again produced the larger yardage total: the Psi Corps had a back who could finish short opportunities without requiring the quarterback to make every decisive throw.

Skattebo added thirty-six receiving yards on two catches. Emmitt Smoth ran five times for twenty-five yards and caught two passes for ten more. Gengar Pickens contributed a seven-yard carry as well as two receptions. Those secondary contributions did not need to dominate the afternoon. They gave Saffron additional useful plays around the lead runner’s work and Manning’s distribution.

“The line made room, and I tried to finish it properly,” Skattebo said. His gentle account leaves the scoring credit where the record puts it while acknowledging the collective work. Nineteen carries for sixty-eight yards is not a runaway rushing display. Two touchdowns on short runs make it a valuable one, especially when the offense can also complete passes to a broad group of receivers.
A late touchdown and a kickoff recovery separated the teams

Manning found Woobat short left for a four-yard touchdown with eleven seconds remaining before halftime. The extra point made it 21–6. Woobat caught one pass in the game and used it to produce six points, which is an excellent way to avoid complaints about target volume. More seriously, the score gave Saffron a fifteen-point lead before Cerulean could reset for the second half.

The reset went badly for the Tide. On the opening kickoff of the third quarter, Zebstrika returned the ball twenty-one yards to the Cerulean twenty-two and fumbled. Ninetales recovered for Saffron. Manning then found HeeDee Lamb deep right for an eleven-yard touchdown at 5:17. The extra point made it 28–6, turning the late-half score and return mistake into a substantial change in the game’s demands.

Zebstrika also caught Cerulean’s second touchdown, another twenty-three-yard reception, this time on a short-left throw at 0:47 of the third. The receiver finished with three catches for fifty-six yards and both of the Tide’s touchdowns. His productive receiving day and costly return fumble both belong in the account. Neither one cancels the other merely because a simpler story would be easier to write.

Saffron’s last points came on Octillery’s thirty-five-yard field goal at 4:32 of the fourth. The Psi Corps had already built enough separation that Cerulean needed repeated scoring possessions. Their defense kept the final quarter scoreless. The game ended with the same basic advantage visible in the first-down totals: Saffron had found substantially more ways to sustain useful offense.
Lamb had help this week

HeeDee Lamb caught five passes for seventy-one yards and a touchdown. That follows his 350-yard performance against Blackthorn, and it should be assessed as its own useful contribution rather than treated as a failure to repeat something extraordinary. Mothel Irving added sixty-four yards on five catches. Bysson Witten had fifty-seven on four. Manning could distribute the work without asking Lamb to carry most of the passing total.

body.alt: Heliolisk #11. HeeDee Lamb caught five passes for seventy-one yards and a touchdown. An editorial receiving illustration.
body.caption: HeeDee Lamb caught five passes for seventy-one yards and a touchdown. An editorial receiving illustration.

body.text: Pawmo’s one reception gained twenty-eight yards. Skattebo added thirty-six, Pickens seventeen and Smoth ten. Woobat supplied the four-yard touchdown. The distribution gave the offense several useful answers at different points in the game. Manning completed two-thirds of his attempts and avoided interceptions, allowing the defense to work with a growing lead rather than respond to abrupt possession changes.

“The right completion can be seven different players,” Manning said. “I’m happy if we keep finding it.” His calm summary is consistent with an afternoon that required patience more than record chasing. The Psi Corps still punted twice and had eleven incomplete passes. Their success came from enough productive snaps to overcome those ordinary interruptions while avoiding the major mistakes that would have helped Cerulean.

Farigiraf completed fourteen of twenty-two for 209 yards, two touchdowns and no interceptions. That is a respectable passing line within a losing performance. The Tide’s rushing total was twenty-seven yards on six attempts, and they converted one of five third downs. Three sacks cost them twenty yards. Cerulean could generate a passing gain without creating enough sustained offense around it to match Saffron’s four touchdowns.
The final game matters differently to each club

Saffron has secured its division and the second seed. The final home game against Fuchsia cannot produce the conference bye, which belongs to Mt. Silver, or move the Psi Corps below second. That gives Scarboro a clear preparation question: how to use the finale to preserve the work his team does well and arrive ready for a first-round opponent that has not yet been settled.

Cerulean hosts Vermilion and needs both its own victory and a particular combination of help elsewhere. Olivine and Violet must both lose for the Tide’s eight-win finish to claim the last place. Cianwood’s result does not change Cerulean’s route. Those are demanding conditions, but they are actual conditions. Calling the Tide finished after this defeat would be as inaccurate as describing their path as comfortable.

Watchog’s new eighteen-week injury designation adds a serious availability problem for Cerulean. The report supports that duration and no more elaborate medical story. Saffron’s own preparation should remain grounded in the current injury list as well, even after a win in which its main offensive contributors supplied substantial work. The playoff field will be built from the players available when those games arrive.

The regular-season finale also gives Saffron another chance to sustain its defensive standard. Fuchsia arrives after a 17–14 defeat at Vermilion, while the Psi Corps have allowed only thirteen points across their last two games.

Scarboro has a final regular-season opponent and a home playoff date to prepare for. Manning has another interception-free performance, Skattebo has two rushing touchdowns, and the defense has kept another opponent below fourteen points. Saffron’s thirteen wins have earned a definite position in the bracket. The remaining task is to make that position useful once the opponent is known.

art.alt: Darmanitan #22. Dam Skattebo scored Saffron’s first two touchdowns in its 31–13 win.

articles.title: Sunyshore gets its passing game back in a 34–7 win
articles.dek: DeZhaun Watzon threw for 305 yards, 88 Special caught two touchdowns, and the Starseekers held Pastoria to five first downs.
articles.author: tessa-wren

body.text: Sunyshore’s passing game recovered its reach, and Pastoria could not create enough offense to keep up. DeZhaun Watzon threw for 305 yards and three touchdowns in a 34–7 road win, with 88 Special catching two scores and Jolt Vick supplying the other. The Starseekers improved to 12–4 as Sinnoh East champions and remained in position to claim the conference’s second seed with a victory in the finale.

The performance followed a 27–3 loss at Mossdeep in which Sunyshore had struggled to sustain offense. This time the Starseekers produced 421 total yards, nineteen first downs and four touchdowns. Pastoria finished with 111 yards and five first downs. The contrast gives Karson Jones useful evidence of a response while preserving the difference in the opponents: a convincing win over the Waves does not replay the game against the unbeaten Eclipse.

Watzon completed twenty-three of thirty-five passes without an interception. 88 Special caught four of five targets for eighty-eight yards and two touchdowns. Jolt Vick had seventy-three yards on five catches, including the opening score. Sunyshore added 116 rushing yards and committed no turnovers, allowing its defense to operate with a lead that grew steadily after a brief second-quarter tie.

“They showed up ready to look like themselves again,” Jones said. “Now I want that confidence to travel with the details attached.” The confidence had a visible foundation: three touchdown passes, six successful third downs and no giveaways. The details still included two sacks allowed and twelve incomplete passes. Jones had enough good work to praise without running out of specific corrections.
Three scoring passes reopened the field

Jolt Vick scored first, catching a deep-middle pass from Watzon for thirty-one yards with 3:16 left in the opening quarter. Duosion’s extra point made it 7–0. The Jolteon’s reception immediately supplied a larger passing play than Sunyshore had been able to turn into a touchdown at Mossdeep. It also gave Pastoria a score to chase before the Waves had established a productive offensive rhythm.

body.alt: Jolteon #24. Jolt Vick scored on a thirty-one-yard deep-middle reception. Illustrated from the recorded play.
body.caption: Jolt Vick scored on a thirty-one-yard deep-middle reception. Illustrated from the recorded play.

body.text: Pastoria did answer. Farigiraf threw short left to Watchog for a three-yard touchdown at 4:22 of the second quarter, and Horsea converted the extra point. The game was tied at seven. That score matters to the shape of the afternoon: Sunyshore’s eventual twenty-seven-point margin came after the opponent had drawn level, rather than from an unbroken procession of unanswered scoring from kickoff.

Watzon moved the Starseekers ahead again with a twenty-two-yard deep-right touchdown to 88 Special at 1:37 of the second. Duosion’s extra point went in off the upright. A thirty-seven-yard field goal with six seconds remaining gave Sunyshore a 17–7 halftime lead. The visitors had recovered the advantage and added points before Pastoria could prepare a second-half response.

The response never reached the scoreboard. Watzon found 88 Special deep right again, this time for twenty-three yards at 4:29 of the third. FLOAT SZN added an eight-yard touchdown run up the middle at 1:25. The Starseekers had turned a ten-point halftime margin into a twenty-four-point lead by the end of the quarter, using both passing and rushing finishes.
The receiving work went beyond the touchdowns

88 Special’s two scoring receptions accounted for forty-five of his eighty-eight yards. His longest catch gained thirty-five. The Sceptile was targeted only five times, making the four completions especially efficient. He provided scoring and yardage without requiring an overwhelming share of Watzon’s attempts. That left room for several teammates to sustain the possessions around his largest plays.

MF STOMP caught seven passes on eleven targets for sixty-three yards. Fera LaGatr added forty on four catches, while BAXXED? gained thirty-nine on two. Jolt Vick’s five receptions supplied another seventy-three. The passing game therefore had a reliable volume target, several secondary contributors and two receivers who finished the touchdown throws. Pastoria had to defend more than one useful route to a gain.

“I got the throws, and I tried to keep the work simple,” 88 Special said. The quiet response suits a player whose receiving line did most of the announcing. Jolt Vick was similarly practical: “Once we got the first one, we still had to do the next possession properly.” Both accounts fit a game that became decisive through repeated useful series rather than one isolated explosive play.

Watzon supplied his own more unusual summary. “It felt like the field had all its doors open again,” he said. “I still had to pick the right one.” The image reflects a productive afternoon, but the measurable part is stronger: 305 passing yards, three touchdowns and no interceptions against a defense that managed only two pass breakups. Sunyshore consistently completed enough attempts to keep its receivers involved.

body.alt: Porygon-Z #30. DeZhaun Watzon threw for 305 yards and three touchdowns. An imagined sideline scene.
body.caption: DeZhaun Watzon threw for 305 yards and three touchdowns. An imagined sideline scene.

body.text: Pastoria’s third downs ended too many possessions

The Waves converted one of nine third downs and punted eight times. Farigiraf completed eight of seventeen passes for sixty-four yards and one touchdown. Four sacks cost twenty-seven yards. Pastoria’s lack of interceptions was a positive, but retaining the ball through a throw did not solve the repeated difficulty of reaching another set of downs.

Oinkologne ran fourteen times for forty-two yards. Watchog added a five-yard carry, bringing Pastoria’s rushing total to forty-seven. The lead runner averaged three yards per attempt, leaving the offense with limited help when the passing game stalled. Arbok led the receivers with twenty-eight yards on two catches, and no other receiver reached twenty yards. The one touchdown drive was not followed by enough similar work.

Sunyshore recorded four sacks, four pass breakups and allowed only five first downs. The defense’s control of the afternoon was broader than any single category. It limited rushing efficiency, interrupted the passing game and repeatedly won third down. With no turnovers providing short scoring opportunities for either club, those sustained differences became the clearest explanation for the final margin.

The Starseekers converted six of eleven third downs. Their offense could therefore continue more than half of those possessions while Pastoria ended nearly all of its own comparable opportunities. Duosion added a twenty-nine-yard field goal in the fourth quarter and finished two for two on field goals, with all four extra points successful. Sunyshore could keep adding points without needing another touchdown to settle the result.
A useful ground game supported the recovery

Myles Gabite carried fifteen times for seventy-two yards. FLOAT SZN added twenty-eight on six attempts and scored the third-quarter rushing touchdown. Jolt Vick gained ten yards on his one carry, and Watzon added six. The combined 116 rushing yards provided enough support that the passing offense could work within a balanced production pattern rather than chase every yard on its own.

Gabite’s longest run gained fourteen yards, while FLOAT SZN’s longest gained nine. That makes the total a record of several useful gains, not one enormous run obscuring a series of failed attempts. Sunyshore had room to keep using the ground game after Watzon’s touchdown passes created separation. The running contributions then helped make the remaining passing assignments less desperate.

The final-round trip to Veilstone gives Sunyshore a clear objective. A win secures the second seed behind Mossdeep. Other results can matter if the Starseekers fail to win, including Petalburg’s finale against Mauville and the tiebreak position among division winners. The current second seed should therefore be described as a position the team can lock down, not an achievement already guaranteed by this victory.

Pastoria travels to Hearthome, where the Haunts still have a route to a wild card. The Waves have been eliminated, but their final result can affect another club’s season. Their immediate corrections are evident in this report: improve the one-for-nine third-down rate, protect Farigiraf from repeated sacks and find more production beyond the one touchdown connection.

Sunyshore leaves with twelve wins, a division title and a passing performance that gives Jones something concrete to carry into the finale. Watzon found three touchdown throws, 88 Special supplied two of them, and the defense forced eight punts. A second-seed finish is now available through one more victory, followed by a home playoff game against an opponent still being decided.

art.alt: Sceptile #88. 88 Special caught two touchdown passes as Sunyshore beat Pastoria 34–7.
